Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Rabbi Jacob Feldman's eyes still widened with a start every time someone touched him without warning. It had been decades since he fled his war-torn homeland as a refugee, but the memories of chaos and violence lingered, etched into his very being. The slightest unexpected brush against his arm or shoulder would send his heart racing, his mind careening back to the rubble-strewn streets where death lurked around every corner. When such moments occurred, Jacob would often retreat into himself, telling himself he deserved to suffer for having survived while others did not. This self-imposed punishment thinking was a familiar refuge, one that distracted him from the overwhelming emotions that threatened to engulf him. He'd busy himself with preparations for upcoming sermons or lose himself in study, avoiding any situation that might lead to emotional closeness with his loved ones – even his wife of over 40 years. The world outside seemed fraught with peril, too. Jacob found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, seeking out a "safe seat" from which he could survey potential dangers. His congregation's synagogue, once a sanctuary, had become one of the few places where he felt truly protected. Even then, his mind would wander to all the ways in which safety was an illusion – how someone else, better equipped or more courageous, might have prevented the horrors he'd witnessed. Jacob couldn't shake the conviction that his body was still on high alert, reacting as if danger lurked around every corner even when logic told him otherwise. "My body remembers," he'd say to himself, "even if my mind doesn't." He felt disconnected from his own thoughts and emotions, uncertain whether he could truly rely on himself in times of crisis. This sense of disconnection was fed by the conviction that others would have coped better with the traumatic events he'd endured. As a rabbi, Jacob had always sought to offer guidance and reassurance to those around him; now, he struggled to find solace for himself. His lack of trust in his own abilities made him even more vigilant, forever on the lookout for potential threats – which only served to further heighten his sensitivity to triggers like unexpected touch or the sight of weapons. When these triggers caught him off guard, Jacob's mind would spiral back into the abyss of memories he'd tried so desperately to keep at bay. The cycle was exhausting: each trigger sparking new waves of self-doubt and fear, which in turn primed him for yet another round of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals. Despite his valiant efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, Jacob's world had grown steadily smaller over the years. His avoidance behaviors, once minor coping mechanisms, had taken on a life of their own – estranging him from loved ones, stifling his passion for teaching, and leaving him feeling isolated in the very community he'd once served with such devotion. The final blow came when Jacob found himself unable to deliver a sermon without breaking down, overcome by the memories that now seemed to assail him from all sides. He realized then that he could no longer continue on this way – that seeking help was not a sign of weakness but a testament to his enduring strength. And so, with a heavy heart and a glimmer of hope, Rabbi Jacob Feldman began the arduous journey toward healing.
